proof.body:
After $k$ completed pair loops, $X=2(Q-k)+r$ and $T=k$. The rank $Q-k$ decreases on each loop. At $k=Q$, the first failed \code{SUB} chooses parity $r$, leaving $X=0,T=Q$. The pair loops cost $3Q$ instructions, the parity exit costs $r+1$, and transferring $T$ back to $X$ costs $2Q+1$. Thus this stage costs $5Q+r+2$ and leaves $X=Q,T=0$.

In the push stage, after $k$ iterations $Y=Y_0-k,T=2k$. Each iteration has three instructions; the rank $Y_0-k$ decreases. The failed exit costs one instruction. Restoring $2Y_0$ tokens from $T$ into $Y$ costs $4Y_0+1$, after which an optional write-one increment costs $w$. This stage costs $7Y_0+2+w$ and leaves $Y=2Y_0+w,T=0$. Adding the costs proves the claim. All loop ranks are natural and strictly decrease when the corresponding loop is taken, so termination holds for arbitrary natural inputs.

At a zero the gates select exactly one branch per step and zero every inactive base. The control interfaces make the branch depart from the current control. The active old interface fixes each retained base: an ordinary counter value for ADD or an unaffected counter, and old value minus one for a positive SUB. The omitted tested base of a zero branch forces its old value to zero. A positive SUB instead requires old value at least one because its base is nonnegative. Hence the active branch is exactly the unique enabled deterministic source branch, and its new forms give the next state.

Starting with natural inputs, every active base and every new counter value is natural, even when the witnesses were allowed to be real. Induction yields exactly the source trace and all witnesses. The last control is $\HALT$. Since $\HALT$ has no outgoing branch, a trace that halted earlier cannot be padded to length $h$. Conversely, the exact halting trace defines the one-hot selectors and the corresponding residual bases uniquely and satisfies every term.
